strengths: The paper presents a very interesting and novel scientific finding: self-supervised speech (SS) representations (particularly the middle layers, such as layer 6 of HuBERT-base) exhibit a strong linear relationship (r = 0.85) with the physical electrical power of muscle action potentials (EMG power). This provides a compelling, grounded explanation of what these speech models implicitly encode.

The dataset collection is a significant contribution: a large-vocabulary, non-invasive EMG-to-speech corpus comprising approximately 9 hours of data across over 6,800 unique words, which will be released to the public.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with clear mathematical formulations of the EMG covariance representations and geodesic distances.
weaknesses: The paper is titled 'emg2speech: synthesizing speech from electromyography...', yet it completely lacks any evaluation of the synthesized speech. No objective metrics of the synthesized audio (such as Mel Cepstral Distortion (MCD), Word Error Rate (WER) using a pretrained ASR model, or character error rate) nor subjective assessments (like Mean Opinion Score (MOS)) are provided. As the authors note in Section 6 ('Continuing work'), these crucial evaluations are left for future work.

Without benchmarking against existing systems (e.g., Gaddy & Klein, 2020/2021) on either phoneme recognition or speech synthesis, it is difficult to calibrate the significance of the reported Unit Error Rate (UER = 58.7%) and Phoneme Error Rate (PER = 41.42%).

While the linear relationship between SS representations and EMG power is beautifully analyzed, the synthesis pipeline does not explicitly leverage this forward mapping. Instead, it relies on training a non-linear sequence-to-sequence network (TDS Conv) to map EMG signals directly to discrete units via CTC loss, making the connection between the analysis and the final synthesis architecture somewhat loose.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly valuable and impactful task: non-invasive speech reconstruction from electromyography (EMG) signals, which has significant clinical applications for individuals with speaking disorders.

The analysis demonstrating a linear relationship between self-supervised speech representations (such as HuBERT layer 6) and physical EMG power vectors provides useful empirical support for why certain layer features work well in downstream speech tasks.
The effort to collect and release a larger, more natural vocabulary EMG speech dataset (9 hours, ~6,800 unique words) is a highly commendable contribution to the research community.
weaknesses: The manuscript is currently incomplete and reads like a work-in-progress draft. Section 6 ('Continuing work') explicitly states that the authors are still developing methods to objectively assess the perceptual quality of the synthesized audio and compute Word Error Rate (WER) and Character Error Rate (CER).

Despite being titled 'emg2speech: synthesizing speech...', the paper provides absolutely no evaluation of the synthesized audio. Standard speech evaluation metrics such as Mel-Cepstral Distortion (MCD), subjective Mean Opinion Scores (MOS), or objective intelligibility metrics (e.g., ESTOI/PESQ or ASR-based WER on synthesized audio) are completely absent.

The quantitative results presented in Tables 1 and 2 show very high error rates (e.g., a Unit Error Rate of 58.7% and a Phoneme Error Rate of 41.42%). Given such high error rates, it is highly likely that the synthesized audio is mostly unintelligible. Without audio evaluations or audio samples, it is impossible to verify if the proposed system actually produces functional speech.

Crucial details regarding the text-to-speech (TTS) vocoder setup are missing. It is unclear if the Tacotron vocoder was trained on the speaker's own acoustic data or on a generic multi-speaker dataset, and how it handles highly corrupted sequences of HuBERT units.

strengths: Presents a valuable scientific contribution by demonstrating a strong linear correlation (r = 0.85) between self-supervised speech representations (specifically layer 6 of HuBERT-base) and the physical power of muscle action potentials, providing a principled articulatory explanation for downstream model performance.

Addresses data scarcity in the field of silent speech and neuromuscular interfaces by collecting a large-vocabulary, 9-hour EMG-to-speech corpus at a natural speaking rate, which is scheduled to be open-sourced.

Employs an alignment-free sequence-to-sequence framework using Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) loss, which is highly practical given that temporal alignment between muscle activity and speech is typically unknown.
weaknesses: Incomplete evaluation of the synthesized audio: Standard speech synthesis and voice conversion metrics (such as Mel-Cepstral Distortion (MCD), PESQ, STOI, and Word Error Rate/Character Error Rate of the reconstructed speech) are missing. As acknowledged in Section 6, these metrics are critical to establishing the perceptual quality and intelligibility of the generated speech.

The description of the primary 9-hour dataset in Section 3 lacks clarity regarding the number of speakers/participants who recorded it. While Section 5.1 mentions 12 participants, footnote 3 clarifies that this was an independent, gesture-only dataset. It is essential to specify the speaker configuration of the main text-to-speech dataset.

The baseline error rates are relatively high (e.g., 41.42% Phoneme Error Rate), suggesting that the generated audio may have limited intelligibility. Without audio samples or demonstration links, it is difficult for reviewers to qualitatively assess the synthesis performance.

strengths: High-impact open-source contribution: Releasing 10 hours of high-quality, continuous EMG-speech data (including clinical data from an ALS patient) is a highly valuable resource for the research community.

Interesting scientific insight: Proving a strong linear mapping (up to r=0.85) between self-supervised speech (S3) representations and physical muscle activity (EMG) offers a strong, articulatory-grounded explanation for why S3 representations are highly effective for speech synthesis.

Clinically realistic framework: Unlike most prior works, this method does not assume time-aligned EMG-audio pairs during training, making it highly applicable to realistic clinical settings where synchronized clean audio is unavailable.

Sound methodology and clear improvements: The introduction of phoneme-guided decoding with cross-head consistency regularization is elegant and yields statistically significant improvements in decoding accuracy.

Rigorous evaluation: The paper features a comprehensive evaluation combining objective metrics, linear probing across various layers of different S3 models, and extensive human-in-the-loop evaluations (WER via transcribers and Mean Opinion Scores).
weaknesses: High Word Error Rates: Although the synthesized speech is acoustically natural (as shown by the MOS), the actual linguistic intelligibility remains relatively low, with human-evaluated Word Error Rates (WER) exceeding 50%.

Limited subject diversity: The dataset only features two participants (one healthy and one clinical). While understandable given the nature of clinical data collection, this limits the ability to assess cross-subject generalization or day-to-day session-to-session variability.

strengths: Compelling scientific probing: The paper establishes a strong, quantitative link (r = 0.85) between self-supervised speech representations (specifically layer 6 of HuBERT-Base) and physical muscle action potentials, offering a principled explanation for why certain S3 layers excel in downstream speech synthesis tasks.

Valuable open-source datasets: The release of a high-quality 9-hour EMG speech dataset (with over 6,800 unique words) alongside a clinically valuable 1-hour corpus from a silent-speaking ALS participant is a major contribution to the open science community.

Methodological innovation: The introduction of phoneme-guided consistency regularization successfully exploits the phonetic alignment of multi-site orofacial muscles to improve discrete speech unit decoding.

High clarity and reproducibility: The paper is exceptionally well-written, with detailed mathematical formulations, comprehensive implementation and optimization parameters, and clear figures of the electrode placements.
weaknesses: High word error rates (WER): Average human transcriber WERs of 62.55% (healthy) and 50.82% (ALS) show that the end-to-end synthesized speech remains highly unintelligible for practical, real-world utility.

Extremely limited participant diversity: The clinical and general-purpose speech datasets rely on a single healthy participant and a single ALS participant, leaving cross-subject generalization and anatomical variance unaddressed.

Lack of direct comparison with competitive benchmarks: Because the work operates in an unaligned (text-only target) setting, it lacks a direct comparison to other established models on a standardized, public benchmark (such as the aligned Gaddy & Klein dataset), making it harder to definitively benchmark the performance of the proposed pipeline.

strengths: High clinical and social relevance: Proposes a non-invasive EMG-based speech neuroprosthesis, addressing the key accessibility, risk, and cost limitations of invasive brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).
High-quality open-source datasets: Releases a massive dataset (9 hours general, 1 hour ALS), addressing a major bottleneck in the EMG-to-speech domain and enabling future reproducible benchmarks.

Strong mechanistic analysis: Establishes a clear, quantitative relationship between self-supervised speech (S3) representations (specifically layer 6 of HuBERT) and physical muscle activity (EMG power), providing a principled explanation of why S3 layers capture articulatory features.
Novel phoneme-guided decoding: Introduces a joint CTC decoding framework that enforces phoneme-unit consistency, yielding statistically significant improvements in unit and phoneme error rates.

Practical and alignment-free setup: Models are trained without requiring parallel, frame-aligned speech/EMG data, which is highly suited for real clinical settings where natural speech may be unavailable or degraded (e.g., silent speech in ALS).
weaknesses: Intelligibility remains limited: Despite the solid acoustic naturalness (as measured by MOS), the human transcription Word Error Rate (WER) remains relatively high (around 50-62%), indicating that further optimization is required for practical, daily clinical utility.

Limited cross-subject and session evaluation: The speech datasets are collected from single subjects (one healthy, one ALS). The robustness of the trained models to cross-subject variations and day-to-day electrode/placement distribution shifts remains uncharacterized.

Lack of direct comparison with other unaligned sequence-to-sequence benchmarks: While the authors reasonably justify why direct comparisons are difficult due to differing data setups and alignment assumptions, contextualizing performance against a broader set of adapted baselines would make the empirical results even stronger.
